St. Petersburg, December 1879. You are an unnamed Third Section investigator, installed in
the private library of a retired censor whose collection has quietly been serving as a safe
house. Somewhere in the Russian Empire, roughly thirty people who call themselves Seraphs
intend to kill Tsar Alexander II at the Blessing of the Waters on the Feast of Theophany,
6 January 1880 — when the Tsar descends to the Neva ice before the Winter Palace. Their
phrase for it: *when the waters are blessed, the fire will descend.*

You never leave the room. What you get is paper — intercepted letters, books pulled from the
shelves, newspapers, a telephone line to people who may or may not tell you the truth — and a
great map of the Empire on an easel with pins and blank cards laid ready beside it. The work
is reading closely and deciding what a sentence is really doing: which alias belongs to which
name, who recruited whom, which of the people in the correspondence are conspirators and which
are innocents whose only crime is proximity.

### What it is

A self-contained detective game that runs in the browser, written and built from scratch —
no engine. The conspiracy has a real internal structure rather than a scripted solution path:
thirty conspirators across three tiers borrowed from Aquinas's account of the seraphim
(*ardor*, *flame*, *ember*), a recruitment tree, operational chains that deliberately do not
match that tree, blood relations, mutual guarantors, and handlers running assets who do not
know they are assets. Twelve innocents are woven through the same correspondence. The evidence
is consistent because it was generated against a single answer key, so the deductions actually
close — and the wrong ones are wrong for findable reasons.

The history is real where it can be. Solovyov's attempt on the Tsar in April 1879, the
founding of Narodnaya Volya that August, the bombing of the imperial train outside Moscow that
November — all present, all in the papers your character reads. The Seraphs are not Narodnaya
Volya and hold them in contempt as godless; they are a heretical-mystical movement convinced
the Tsar has usurped a sacrality belonging to God alone. The press of the day confuses the two,
which is a mistake the game lets you make as well.

### Built with

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript — no framework and no build step. The library, the map and the
documents are all drawn as generated SVG, the type is self-hosted, and the score is public-domain
Bach, Beethoven, Chopin and Mussorgsky. It ships as static files.
